items.title: Aggressive driving: what it is
items.simple: An aggressive driver breaks traffic laws on purpose to scare, bother, hurt or block others. They tailgate, weave, speed, run red lights and pass on the shoulder.
items.official: Defined by Virginia law as the intent to harass, intimidate, injure or obstruct another person while committing one or more traffic offenses such as failing to stop or yield the right-of-way, avoiding a traffic control device or failing to give way to an overtaking vehicle. Aggressive drivers run stop signs and red lights, speed, tailgate, weave in and out of traffic, pass on the right (including on the shoulder and unpaved portions of the road), make improper and unsafe lane changes, make hand and facial gestures, scream, honk and flash their lights.

items.title: Stay away from aggressive drivers
items.simple: If you see an aggressive driver, stay out of the way. Do not speed up or race them. Do not look them in the eye. Ignore their yelling and hand signs.
items.official: Protect yourself. If you see an aggressive driver, stay out of the way. Don't challenge the aggressive driver by speeding up or trying to out-maneuver him. Avoid eye contact and ignore his gestures and shouting.
items.mnemonic: Don't race, don't face. Let them pass.

items.title: Aggressive driving: 10 days-6 months
items.simple: Convicted (found guilty) of aggressive driving? You can lose your license. It can be for 10 days, or as long as 6 months.
items.official: If you are convicted of aggressive driving, your license could be suspended for ten days or for as long as six months.
items.mnemonic: Road rage costs 10 days up to half a year (6 months).

items.title: Many things can distract you
items.simple: Driving needs all of your attention. These can distract you: music, GPS, passengers, eating, phones and sights outside.
items.official: Driving requires your full attention. There are many distractions that may prevent drivers from focusing on driving: changing the music selection/podcast/GPS, talking to passengers, observing outside surroundings, eating, using a cell phone and more.

items.title: No holding a phone
items.simple: In Virginia, you may not hold a phone while you drive. There are two exceptions: a driver emergency, or your car is legally parked or stopped.
items.official: Virginia law prohibits drivers from holding cell phones or any other wireless communication devices while driving except in a driver emergency or the vehicle is lawfully parked or stopped.
items.mnemonic: Hands on the wheel, phone out of hand.

items.title: Phone GPS: no holding or typing
items.simple: You may use a phone for directions (GPS) while you drive. But you may not hold it. You may not type into it. Set it up before you go.
items.official: A mobile phone or other telecommunications device may be used for navigation, as long as the driver is not entering information or holding it while driving.
items.mnemonic: GPS: set it, then forget it.

items.title: Distraction: 17% of crashes
items.simple: Distraction causes about 17 percent of all crashes in Virginia each year. While you look away, your car can drift into danger. You lose seconds you need to react.
items.official: Annually, driver distraction accounts for roughly 17 percent of all traffic crashes in Virginia. While the driver is distracted, the vehicle may move into a high risk situation. The driver then loses precious seconds before recognizing the situation and must make an emergency maneuver. Young distracted drivers are even more susceptible. Failure to maintain proper control, following too closely, and not yielding the right-of-way are common actions of young distracted drivers.

items.title: Eyes on road, hands on wheel
items.simple: Keep your eyes on the road and your hands on the wheel. Set up controls and devices before you drive. Do not use a phone. To do something distracting, pull over and stop first.
items.official: Drivers should not use cell phones, computers or other distracting devices except to report a crash or emergency. Before engaging in distracting behavior, pull over and stop the vehicle in a safe location. Keep your eyes on the road and your hands on the wheel at all times. Set or adjust the controls on the vehicle and other devices as soon as you get in the car and before you begin driving. Do not use a cell phone.

items.title: Signs you are too sleepy
items.simple: Watch for sleepy signs. You yawn a lot, nod your head, or have heavy eyelids. You forget the last few miles. You miss exits, drift lanes or hit rumble strips.
items.official: Constant yawning, head nodding, heavy eyelids, difficulty remembering the last few miles driven, missing road signs or exits, unplanned lane changes, driving off the road or hitting rumble strips are all signs of drowsy driving. Driving while you are sleepy increases your crash risk as you struggle to process complex information coming from different places at once. You may make careless driving decisions, have trouble paying attention or actually fall asleep while driving. Drowsy driving is a type of impaired driving.
items.mnemonic: Yawn, nod, drift? Time to stop.

items.title: Prevent drowsy driving
items.simple: Before a trip, get plenty of good sleep. Skip alcohol and heavy foods. Watch out for medicines that affect driving. If you can, bring a friend and switch drivers. Always let a well-rested person drive.
items.official: To avoid drowsy driving: get plenty of quality sleep before a trip; avoid alcoholic beverages and heavy foods; beware of medications that can impair your driving ability; if possible, drive with a companion and switch drivers when necessary. Always let a well-rested person drive.

items.title: Rest every two hours
items.simple: Limit long drives. On a long trip, stop to rest at least every two hours.
items.official: Limit long distance driving. Stop at least every two hours for rest.
items.mnemonic: Two hours, take a rest.

items.title: A 10-20 minute nap helps
items.simple: If you are sleepy, stop at a safe place and take a nap. Just 10 to 20 minutes of sleep can make a big difference.
items.official: Stop at a safe place and take a nap. As little as 10 to 20 minutes of sleep can make a big difference.
items.mnemonic: Sleepy? Stop and nap 10 to 20 minutes.

items.title: Avoid driving 10 p.m.-6 a.m.
items.simple: To avoid drowsy driving, try not to drive between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m.
items.official: To avoid drowsy driving: Avoid driving from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.
items.mnemonic: 10 to 6: sleep, don't drive.

items.title: Coffee and radio don't fix sleepy
items.simple: Open windows, gum, a loud radio, coffee and energy drinks do NOT stop drowsy driving. You cannot count on them to keep you awake. Stop and rest instead.
items.official: Rolling down a window, chewing gum, turning up the radio, or consuming caffeine, energy drinks or other stimulants do not prevent drowsy driving and are not reliable methods for staying awake.
items.mnemonic: Gum, radio, window, coffee: no. Rest: yes.

items.title: See a drowsy driver? Report it
items.simple: See a drowsy driver? Find a safe place to stop, or ask a passenger to call police. Be ready to tell them where, what car, and what it did.
items.official: If you observe a drowsy driver, find a safe place to stop or ask a passenger to call law enforcement. Be able to describe the location, vehicle and actions you observed.
items.mnemonic: Tell police 3 things: where, what car, what it did.

items.title: Age 21+: DUI at .08 BAC
items.simple: BAC means blood alcohol content. Are you 21 or older? Then a BAC of .08 or higher is DUI. DUI means driving under the influence.
items.official: Legally, drivers age 21 or older are considered to be driving under the influence (DUI) if your blood alcohol content (BAC) is .08 percent or higher.
items.mnemonic: 21 and over: .08 is a DUI.

items.title: Under .08 can still be DUI
items.simple: Is your BAC under .08? You can still get a DUI. If alcohol makes your driving impaired, that is enough.
items.official: If your driving is impaired, you can be convicted of driving under the influence with a BAC lower than .08 percent.
items.mnemonic: Under .08 is not a free pass.

items.title: Under 21: .02 BAC is illegal
items.simple: Under 21? A BAC of .02 to just under .08 counts as illegal drinking. At .08 or higher, you could get a DUI.
items.official: If under age 21, you can be convicted of illegal consumption of alcohol if your BAC is at least .02 but less than .08. If your BAC is .08 or higher you could be convicted of a DUI.
items.mnemonic: Under 21: .02 and you're through.

items.title: Late night: 3 in 10 drunk
items.simple: Between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m., about 3 out of every 10 drivers are drunk. More than 1 in 3 of them drank at someone else's home. In your life, you have a 50-50 chance of an alcohol-related crash.
items.official: Researchers estimate that between the hours of 10 PM and 2 AM three out of every ten drivers are drunk. More than one-third of these drivers have been drinking at someone else's home. Nearly 50 percent of the drivers arrested for DUI are social to moderate drinkers. In your lifetime, there's a 50-50 chance that you'll be involved in an alcohol-related crash.
items.mnemonic: 10 to 2: 3 in 10 are drunk.

items.title: One drink changes your driving
items.simple: Just one drink can hurt your driving. Even a little alcohol affects your brain. It harms your vision, your judgment and your coordination.
items.official: Just one alcoholic drink can affect your driving ability because even a small amount of alcohol affects the brain's functions - particularly vision, judgment, and coordination.
items.mnemonic: One drink hurts how you See, Think and Move (vision, judgment, coordination).

items.title: Drinking: 7 times crash risk
items.simple: Driving after drinking makes a crash 7 times more likely than driving sober.
items.official: Because alcohol affects your judgment and driving ability, your chances of being in a crash are seven times greater if you drive after drinking than if you drive sober.
items.mnemonic: Drink and drive: 7 times the risk.

items.title: Beer, shot, wine: same alcohol
items.simple: One 12-ounce beer is the same as one shot of liquor. It is also the same as one 5-ounce glass of wine. A beer counts as much as a shot.
items.official: Twelve ounces of beer is the same as a shot of liquor or a five-ounce glass of wine.
items.mnemonic: 12-5-1: a 12-ounce beer = a 5-ounce wine = 1 shot.

items.title: Only time sobers you up
items.simple: Only time can sober you up. Coffee will not. A cold shower will not. Exercise will not.
items.official: Only time can decrease intoxication. Coffee, cold showers or exercise will not sober you up.
items.mnemonic: No shortcut: only time.

items.title: Decide before you drink
items.simple: Alcohol crashes are not accidents. They can be prevented. Decide before you drink that you will not drive. Plan a sober ride home. Deciding gets harder after one or two drinks.
items.official: Alcohol-related crashes are not accidents. They can be prevented! The only way to avoid the risks of drinking and driving is to decide before you start drinking that you are not going to drive. Making the decision not to drive is a lot more difficult after one or two drinks. When attending a social event where alcohol will be consumed, plan ahead for a sober ride home by using alternative transportation or having a sober driver.
items.mnemonic: Plan the ride before the drink.

items.title: Alcohol plus drugs multiplies
items.simple: Mixing alcohol with other drugs usually multiplies the effects of both. One drink plus another drug can affect you like several drinks. Even aspirin or cold medicine counts.
items.official: Combining alcohol with other drugs usually multiplies the effects of both and can have a disastrous effect on your ability to drive. One drink taken when you are on another drug - even an aspirin, or allergy or cold medicine - could have the same effect on your driving ability as drinking several alcoholic beverages.
items.mnemonic: Mix means multiply.

items.title: Medicine can affect driving
items.simple: Many store-bought and prescription medicines can make you sleepy or dizzy. This includes pills, syrups, drops and sprays. Read the label. If you are not sure, ask a pharmacist or doctor.
items.official: Almost any drug can reduce your ability to drive safely. It's not just illegal drugs that cause problems. Many over-the-counter medications and prescription drugs for headaches, hay fever, colds, allergies or nervous conditions can cause drowsiness and dizziness. This includes syrups, drops, sprays, pills and tablets. They often affect driver alertness and slow reaction time. Read the label before taking any drug or medicine. Look for warnings about side effects. If you're uncertain about the effects of a drug, ask your pharmacist or doctor. No drug is harmless.
items.mnemonic: No drug is harmless. Read the label first.

items.title: Drugged driving is DUI too
items.simple: Any drug that harms your driving can bring the same penalties as drunk driving. Adults over 21 may legally have marijuana. But driving high is still illegal.
items.official: If your driving is impaired because you are under the influence of any drug, you may face the same penalties as driving under the influence of alcohol. Although the possession of marijuana and marijuana products (over the age of 21) is legal, driving under the influence of marijuana is still illegal. Smoking or consuming cannabis will affect how you drive.
items.mnemonic: Legal to have is not legal to drive.

items.title: Implied consent: breath test
items.simple: Drive on Virginia's public roads, and you agree to a breath test if police ask. This is implied consent. After a crash, police with probable cause can arrest you for DUI within 3 hours. No warrant needed.
items.official: If the police have probable cause to stop you and suspect that you have been drinking or using drugs, they will ask you to take a breath or blood test. Under implied consent laws, if you operate a motor vehicle on Virginia's public roads, you agree to take a breath test upon request. If you are involved in a motor vehicle crash and a law enforcement officer has probable cause, you can be arrested for DUI within three hours of the crash without a warrant and at any location.
items.mnemonic: Drive here, agree to blow. After a crash: 3 hours, no warrant.

items.title: Automatic suspension: 7 days first
items.simple: Refuse a breath test, or get charged with DUI at .08 or more? You lose your license automatically. First offense: 7 days. Second: 60 days or until trial. Third: until trial.
items.official: If you refuse a breath test or your BAC is .08 percent or higher while you are driving and law enforcement charges you with DUI, your driving privilege will be automatically suspended: for seven days, for a first offense; for 60 days or until you go to trial, whichever comes first, for a second offense; until the trial, for a third DUI offense. If you are convicted of DUI, the court and DMV will impose a suspension/revocation and other penalties in addition to the administrative license suspension. If you receive multiple DUI convictions, the suspension/revocation periods will run consecutively.
items.mnemonic: 7 days, then 60, then trial.

items.title: Open container: passenger area
items.simple: Police stop you. An open, partly empty alcohol container is in the passenger area. You show signs of drinking. Then police can charge you with drinking while driving. An unlocked glove box counts as the passenger area.
items.official: You may be charged with drinking while operating a motor vehicle if you are stopped by law enforcement and you have an open container of alcohol in the passenger area and the contents have been partially removed, and show signs that you have been drinking. The passenger area means the area that seats the driver and passengers and any area within the driver's reach, including an unlocked glove compartment.
items.mnemonic: If the driver can reach it, it counts. Even an unlocked glove box.

items.title: DUI with a child: extra penalty
items.simple: DUI with a child (age 17 or younger) in the car? You must spend 5 extra days in jail. You may also pay an extra $500 to $1,000. A second offense adds 80 hours of community service.
items.official: Conviction of any DUI offense involving a juvenile passenger (age 17 or younger) in the vehicle at the time of the offense carries an additional mandatory five-day jail term plus all other fines and jail sentences. You may also be charged an additional fine of at least $500 and up to $1,000. A second DUI offense with a juvenile in the vehicle carries an additional 80-hour community service requirement.
items.mnemonic: Kid in the car: plus 5 days jail, plus $500 to $1,000.

items.title: Car impounded 30 days
items.simple: Is your license suspended for an alcohol offense, and you drive anyway? Your car is taken away (impounded) for 30 days, right away. If you are convicted, the court can keep it 90 more days.
items.official: Your vehicle will be impounded immediately for 30 days if you are caught driving after your license has been suspended for an alcohol-related offense. The court can impound the vehicle for an additional 90 days if you are convicted. If you drive without a license after a previous conviction for driving without a license, the vehicle is impounded until you obtain a license or for three days, whichever is less.
items.mnemonic: 30 now, 90 more if convicted.

items.title: DUI crash: pay up to $1,000
items.simple: Did your DUI cause a crash? You may have to pay for the police, EMS, firefighters and rescue workers who came. It can cost up to $1,000. It depends on the city or county.
items.official: Depending on the laws of the city or county in which you are driving, you may be responsible for paying the cost (up to $1,000) for law enforcement, emergency medical services, fire fighters and rescue personnel who respond to a crash or incident resulting from your DUI violation.

items.title: Under 21: lose license 1 year
items.simple: Under 21, you cannot buy, have or drink alcohol. Convicted of driving with a BAC of .02 to under .08? You lose your license for 1 year. You also pay at least $500 or do 50 hours of community service.
items.official: If you are under age 21, you cannot purchase, possess or consume alcohol. If you are convicted of driving after illegally consuming alcohol, and your BAC was at least .02 percent and less than .08 percent, the court penalty will include a suspension of your driving privilege for one year from the date of conviction, and a minimum mandatory fine of $500, or the requirement that you complete at least 50 hours of community service. Virginia has a zero tolerance law against underage drinking. If you are convicted of driving after illegally consuming alcohol and your BAC was .08 percent or higher, you may face the same penalties as an adult.
items.mnemonic: Zero tolerance: 1 year off the road, plus $500 OR 50 hours.

items.title: Giving alcohol to under 21
items.simple: Never give or sell alcohol to anyone under 21 or anyone drunk. Or to anyone a court told not to drink. Fine: up to $2,500. Jail: 12 months. License: lost up to 1 year.
items.official: If you provide or sell alcoholic beverages to a person under age 21 or someone who is intoxicated or ordered by a court to refrain from drinking alcohol, you are subject to a fine up to $2,500, mandatory suspension of your driver's license for up to one year, and 12 months in jail.

items.title: Fake ID: big penalties
items.simple: Use a fake ID to get alcohol when under 21? Fine: at least $500. Service: at least 50 hours. Jail: up to 12 months. License: lost for 6 months to 1 year.
items.official: If you are under age 21 and you use or attempt to use a fake ID to establish a false age in an attempt to drink or purchase alcohol, you will: be fined at least $500; be required to perform at least 50 hours of community service; face up to 12 months in jail; and face mandatory suspension of your driver's license for at least six months but not more than one year.
items.mnemonic: Fake ID: $500 AND 50 hours. (Under-21 drinking is $500 OR 50 hours.)

events.prompt: Fine for giving alcohol to someone under 21?
events.missLine: Providing alcohol to someone under 21 can bring a fine up to $2,500.

events.prompt: Give alcohol to someone under 21: license lost up to:
events.missLine: Giving alcohol to someone under 21 can cost your license for up to 1 year.

events.prompt: Fake ID: license lost for how long?
events.missLine: A fake ID brings a license suspension of 6 months to 1 year.

events.prompt: Fake ID: the fine is at least:
events.missLine: Using a fake ID to get alcohol means a fine of at least $500.

events.prompt: Fake ID: community service of at least:
events.missLine: Using a fake ID to get alcohol means at least 50 hours of community service.

questions.prompt: Virginia law defines aggressive driving as committing traffic offenses with the intent to:
choices: Harass, intimidate, injure or obstruct another person
questions.explain: Aggressive driving means breaking traffic laws to harass, scare, hurt or block another person.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of aggressive driving?
choices: Passing on the right using the shoulder
Dimming your headlights for oncoming cars
questions.explain: Passing on the right, including on the shoulder, is an aggressive driving behavior.

questions.prompt: Aggressive drivers often:
choices: Tailgate, weave in and out of traffic and flash their lights
questions.explain: Aggressive drivers tailgate, weave, speed, run red lights, honk and flash their lights.

questions.prompt: Under Virginia law, aggressive driving includes the intent to harass or intimidate while committing a traffic offense such as:
choices: Driving with your low beams on in rain
Failing to stop or yield the right-of-way
questions.explain: Failing to stop or yield the right-of-way is one of the offenses named in the aggressive driving law.

questions.prompt: If you see an aggressive driver, you should:
choices: Speed up so they cannot pass
Make eye contact so they know you see them
Stay out of the way and avoid eye contact
questions.explain: Stay out of the way, do not challenge them, and avoid eye contact.

questions.prompt: An aggressive driver is making gestures and shouting at you. You should:
choices: Slow down in front of them to teach a lesson
questions.explain: Ignore an aggressive driver's gestures and shouting and stay out of their way.

questions.prompt: If you are convicted of aggressive driving, your license could be suspended for:
questions.explain: An aggressive driving conviction can bring a suspension of ten days up to six months.

questions.prompt: The longest license suspension for an aggressive driving conviction is:
questions.explain: Aggressive driving can bring a license suspension for as long as six months.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a driving distraction?
questions.explain: Music, GPS, passengers, eating, phones and outside sights can all distract a driver.

questions.prompt: Driving requires:
choices: Attention only when passengers are quiet
questions.explain: Driving requires your full attention at all times.

questions.prompt: Virginia law prohibits drivers from holding a cell phone while driving except:
choices: In a driver emergency or when the vehicle is lawfully parked or stopped
When talking to a family member
questions.explain: You may not hold a phone while driving unless there is a driver emergency or you are lawfully parked or stopped.

questions.prompt: In Virginia, holding a cell phone or other wireless device while driving is:
choices: Allowed if you use only one hand
Against the law, except in a driver emergency or when lawfully parked or stopped
questions.explain: Virginia law prohibits holding a wireless device while driving except in an emergency or when lawfully parked or stopped.

questions.prompt: A phone may be used for navigation while driving as long as the driver:
choices: Is going under the speed limit
Has a passenger in the car
Is not entering information or holding it
questions.explain: Navigation is allowed only if the driver is not entering information or holding the device.

questions.prompt: Which of these is allowed while driving in Virginia?
choices: Typing an address into your phone's GPS
Following phone navigation without holding it or entering information
Holding your phone to read a map
questions.explain: You may use a phone for navigation if you do not hold it or enter information while driving.

questions.prompt: Each year, driver distraction accounts for roughly what percent of all traffic crashes in Virginia?
questions.explain: Driver distraction accounts for roughly 17 percent of all traffic crashes in Virginia each year.

questions.prompt: Distracted driving is so dangerous because:
choices: Phones use power from the car battery
It makes the engine work harder
It is only illegal at night
The vehicle may move into a high-risk situation and the driver loses precious seconds
questions.explain: While you are distracted, your vehicle can move into danger before you notice.

questions.prompt: Common actions of young distracted drivers include:
choices: Failing to maintain control, following too closely and not yielding
Stopping too long at stop signs
questions.explain: Young distracted drivers often fail to keep control, follow too closely and fail to yield.

questions.prompt: Before engaging in distracting behavior while driving, you should:
choices: Turn on your hazard lights and keep going
Pull over and stop in a safe location
questions.explain: Before doing anything distracting, pull over and stop in a safe place.

questions.prompt: Drivers should not use cell phones on the road except to:
choices: Read a text in slow traffic
questions.explain: Use a phone on the road only to report a crash or emergency.

questions.prompt: To avoid distracted driving, you should:
choices: Set or adjust vehicle controls and devices before you begin driving
questions.explain: Set up your controls and devices before you start driving, and keep your eyes on the road.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a sign of drowsy driving?
questions.explain: Yawning, heavy eyelids and missing signs or exits are all signs of drowsy driving.

questions.prompt: Hitting rumble strips and making unplanned lane changes are signs that you may be:
questions.explain: Drifting, unplanned lane changes and hitting rumble strips are signs of drowsy driving.

questions.prompt: Drowsy driving is:
choices: Safe with the window rolled down
questions.explain: Drowsy driving is a type of impaired driving.

questions.prompt: Driving while you are sleepy increases your crash risk because you may:
questions.explain: A sleepy driver may make careless decisions, have trouble paying attention or fall asleep at the wheel.

questions.prompt: To avoid drowsy driving, you should:
choices: Eat a large, heavy meal before driving
Get plenty of quality sleep before a trip
Drive late at night when roads are empty
questions.explain: Getting plenty of quality sleep before a trip helps prevent drowsy driving.

questions.prompt: If you drive with a companion on a long trip, you should:
choices: Switch drivers when necessary and let a well-rested person drive
Let the tired driver keep going to save time
questions.explain: Switch drivers when needed and always let a well-rested person drive.

questions.prompt: Which can help prevent drowsy driving?
choices: Avoiding alcoholic beverages and heavy foods
questions.explain: Avoiding alcohol and heavy foods helps; gum, a loud radio and open windows do not.

questions.prompt: On a long trip, you should stop for rest at least every:
questions.explain: Limit long distance driving and stop at least every two hours for rest.

questions.prompt: To limit long distance driving and avoid drowsiness, you should:
choices: Stop only when you need gas
Stop at least every two hours for rest
Drive straight through to save time
questions.explain: Stop at least every two hours for rest on a long trip.

questions.prompt: If you feel drowsy while driving, you should:
choices: Roll down the window and keep going
Stop at a safe place and take a nap
questions.explain: Stop at a safe place and take a nap; even 10 to 20 minutes can help.

questions.prompt: As little as how much sleep can make a big difference for a drowsy driver?
questions.explain: As little as 10 to 20 minutes of sleep can make a big difference.

questions.prompt: To avoid drowsy driving, try not to drive between:
questions.explain: Avoid driving from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. to help prevent drowsy driving.

questions.prompt: Which time period should you avoid driving to prevent drowsy driving?
questions.explain: Avoid driving from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a reliable way to prevent drowsy driving?
choices: Drinking coffee or an energy drink
questions.explain: Open windows, loud radios and caffeine are not reliable ways to stay awake.

questions.prompt: Chewing gum, turning up the radio and drinking caffeine:
choices: Are reliable ways to stay awake
questions.explain: Gum, radio and caffeine do not prevent drowsy driving and are not reliable.

questions.prompt: If you observe a drowsy driver, you should:
choices: Find a safe place to stop or ask a passenger to call law enforcement
Flash your high beams at them
questions.explain: Find a safe place to stop or have a passenger call law enforcement.

questions.prompt: When you report a drowsy driver, you should be able to describe:
choices: The location, vehicle and actions you observed
questions.explain: Be able to describe the location, vehicle and actions you observed.

questions.prompt: Drivers age 21 or older are considered to be driving under the influence if their BAC is:
questions.explain: For drivers 21 or older, a BAC of .08 percent or higher is DUI.

questions.prompt: For a driver age 21 or older, a BAC of .08 percent or higher means the driver is:
choices: Safe to drive if they feel fine
questions.explain: A BAC of .08 percent or higher is DUI for drivers 21 or older.

questions.prompt: If your driving is impaired, you can be convicted of driving under the influence:
choices: Only if your BAC is .08 or higher
Only if you refuse a breath test
Even with a BAC lower than .08 percent
Only if you cause a crash
questions.explain: Impaired driving can be a DUI even when your BAC is below .08 percent.

questions.prompt: A driver with a BAC below .08 percent:
choices: Can never be charged with DUI
Can only get a parking ticket
Can still be convicted of DUI if their driving is impaired
questions.explain: You can be convicted of DUI with a BAC under .08 if your driving is impaired.

questions.prompt: If you are under 21, you can be convicted of illegal consumption of alcohol if your BAC is:
questions.explain: Under 21, a BAC of at least .02 but less than .08 is illegal consumption of alcohol.

questions.prompt: A driver under age 21 whose BAC is .08 or higher:
choices: Cannot be charged because of age
Is charged only if a crash happens
questions.explain: An under-21 driver with a BAC of .08 or higher could be convicted of DUI.

questions.prompt: Researchers estimate that between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m., how many drivers are drunk?
questions.explain: Between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m., about three out of every ten drivers are drunk.

questions.prompt: In your lifetime, your chance of being involved in an alcohol-related crash is:
questions.explain: There is a 50-50 chance you will be in an alcohol-related crash in your lifetime.

questions.prompt: Nearly 50 percent of drivers arrested for DUI are:
questions.explain: Nearly half of drivers arrested for DUI are social to moderate drinkers.

questions.prompt: Even a small amount of alcohol affects the brain's functions, particularly:
questions.explain: Even a little alcohol affects vision, judgment and coordination.

questions.prompt: How many alcoholic drinks can affect your driving ability?
questions.explain: Just one alcoholic drink can affect your driving ability.

questions.prompt: Your chances of being in a crash are how many times greater if you drive after drinking than if you drive sober?
questions.explain: Driving after drinking makes your chance of a crash seven times greater than driving sober.

questions.prompt: Compared to driving sober, driving after drinking makes your chance of a crash:
questions.explain: Your crash chance is seven times greater if you drive after drinking.

questions.prompt: Twelve ounces of beer is the same as:
choices: A shot of liquor or a five-ounce glass of wine
questions.explain: Twelve ounces of beer equals a shot of liquor or a five-ounce glass of wine.

questions.prompt: Which is the same as a five-ounce glass of wine?
questions.explain: A five-ounce glass of wine is the same as twelve ounces of beer or one shot of liquor.

questions.prompt: The only thing that can decrease intoxication is:
questions.explain: Only time can decrease intoxication.

questions.prompt: A person who has been drinking can sober up faster by:
choices: None of these; only time works
questions.explain: Coffee, cold showers and exercise will not sober you up; only time works.

questions.prompt: The only way to avoid the risks of drinking and driving is to:
choices: Decide before you start drinking that you are not going to drive
Drive slowly with hazard lights on
questions.explain: Decide before you start drinking that you will not drive.

questions.prompt: Alcohol-related crashes:
choices: Are not accidents and can be prevented
questions.explain: Alcohol-related crashes are not accidents; they can be prevented.

questions.prompt: When attending a social event where alcohol will be served, you should:
choices: Plan ahead for a sober ride home
questions.explain: Plan ahead for a sober driver or another way to get home.

questions.prompt: Combining alcohol with other drugs:
choices: Usually multiplies the effects of both
questions.explain: Alcohol with other drugs usually multiplies the effects of both.

questions.prompt: One drink taken with a drug such as aspirin, or allergy or cold medicine:
choices: Could affect your driving like several alcoholic drinks
Is safe if you drive slowly
questions.explain: One drink plus another drug can affect your driving like several drinks.

questions.prompt: Over-the-counter and prescription drugs for colds, allergies or headaches:
choices: Make you a more alert driver
questions.explain: Many over-the-counter and prescription drugs can cause drowsiness and dizziness.

questions.prompt: If you are uncertain about the effects of a drug, you should:
choices: Take a double dose to test it
Drive a short distance to see
questions.explain: Ask your pharmacist or doctor if you are unsure how a drug will affect you.

questions.prompt: Which statement about drugs and driving is true?
choices: Syrups and sprays are always safe
questions.explain: Almost any drug can reduce your ability to drive safely; no drug is harmless.

questions.prompt: If your driving is impaired because of any drug, you:
choices: Face no penalty if the drug is legal
May face the same penalties as driving under the influence of alcohol
Face penalties only if you crash
questions.explain: Drug-impaired driving can bring the same penalties as alcohol DUI.

questions.prompt: For adults over 21 in Virginia, possessing marijuana is legal. Driving under its influence is:
choices: Legal if under the speed limit
questions.explain: Driving under the influence of marijuana is still illegal.

questions.prompt: Under Virginia's implied consent law, if you drive on Virginia's public roads you agree to:
choices: Take a breath test upon request
Take a road test every year
questions.explain: Under implied consent, driving on public roads means you agree to a breath test upon request.

questions.prompt: If you are in a crash and an officer has probable cause, you can be arrested for DUI without a warrant up to how long after the crash?
questions.explain: You can be arrested for DUI within three hours of a crash without a warrant.

questions.prompt: After a crash, an officer with probable cause can arrest you for DUI:
choices: Within three hours of the crash, without a warrant, at any location
questions.explain: You can be arrested within three hours of the crash without a warrant and at any location.

questions.prompt: If police have probable cause to stop you and suspect you have been drinking or using drugs, they will ask you to:
choices: Take a breath or blood test
questions.explain: Police who suspect drinking or drug use will ask you to take a breath or blood test.

questions.prompt: For a first offense, the automatic license suspension after a breath test refusal or a DUI charge (BAC .08 or higher) lasts:
questions.explain: A first offense brings an automatic seven-day license suspension.

questions.prompt: For a second DUI offense, the administrative license suspension lasts:
choices: 60 days or until trial, whichever comes first
questions.explain: A second offense means suspension for 60 days or until trial, whichever comes first.

questions.prompt: For a third DUI offense, the administrative license suspension lasts:
questions.explain: A third DUI offense means your license is suspended until the trial.

questions.prompt: If you receive multiple DUI convictions, the suspension/revocation periods:
questions.explain: With multiple DUI convictions, the suspension/revocation periods run consecutively.

questions.prompt: For open container laws, the passenger area of a vehicle includes:
choices: Any area within the driver's reach, including an unlocked glove compartment
questions.explain: The passenger area is the seating area plus any area within the driver's reach, including an unlocked glove compartment.

questions.prompt: You may be charged with drinking while operating a motor vehicle if you are stopped and:
choices: A sealed container is in the locked trunk
An open alcohol container in the passenger area is partly empty and you show signs of drinking
You have a receipt for alcohol
questions.explain: An open, partly empty container in the passenger area plus signs of drinking can bring this charge.

questions.prompt: A DUI conviction with a passenger age 17 or younger in the vehicle adds a mandatory jail term of:
questions.explain: A DUI with a juvenile passenger adds a mandatory five-day jail term.

questions.prompt: If you are convicted of DUI with a juvenile in the vehicle, you may be charged an additional fine of:
questions.explain: An additional fine of at least $500 and up to $1,000 may be charged.

questions.prompt: A second DUI offense with a juvenile in the vehicle carries an additional:
questions.explain: A second DUI with a juvenile aboard adds 80 hours of community service.

questions.prompt: If you drive while your license is suspended for an alcohol-related offense, your vehicle is impounded immediately for:
questions.explain: Your vehicle is impounded immediately for 30 days.

questions.prompt: If you are convicted of driving on an alcohol-related suspension, the court can impound your vehicle for an additional:
questions.explain: The court can impound the vehicle for an additional 90 days.

questions.prompt: If you drive without a license after a prior conviction for driving without a license, your vehicle is impounded:
choices: Until you get a license or for three days, whichever is less
questions.explain: The vehicle stays impounded until you get a license or for three days, whichever is less.

questions.prompt: After a crash caused by your DUI violation, you may have to pay up to how much for emergency responders' costs?
questions.explain: You may have to pay up to $1,000 for the emergency responders.

questions.prompt: Restitution for a DUI crash may pay the cost of:
choices: Law enforcement, emergency medical services, firefighters and rescue personnel
questions.explain: You may have to pay for the police, EMS, firefighters and rescue personnel who respond.

questions.prompt: A driver under 21 convicted of driving with a BAC of at least .02 but less than .08 will have their license suspended for:
questions.explain: The court suspends the license for one year from the date of conviction.

questions.prompt: Besides the suspension, an under-21 driver convicted of illegal consumption must pay a minimum $500 fine or complete at least:
questions.explain: The penalty includes a $500 minimum fine or at least 50 hours of community service.

questions.prompt: Virginia's law against underage drinking is a:
questions.explain: Virginia has a zero tolerance law against underage drinking.

questions.prompt: If you are under age 21, Virginia law says you cannot:
questions.explain: If you are under 21, you cannot purchase, possess or consume alcohol.

questions.prompt: If you provide or sell alcohol to a person under age 21, you are subject to a fine of up to:
questions.explain: Providing alcohol to someone under 21 can bring a fine of up to $2,500.

questions.prompt: Providing alcoholic beverages to a person who is intoxicated can result in:
choices: A fine up to $2,500, license suspension up to one year, and 12 months in jail
questions.explain: Providing alcohol to an intoxicated person brings the same penalties as providing it to someone under 21.

questions.prompt: If you are under 21 and use a fake ID to try to buy alcohol, your license will be suspended for:
choices: At least six months but not more than one year
questions.explain: A fake ID conviction brings a license suspension of six months to one year.

questions.prompt: The penalty for a person under 21 who uses a fake ID to buy alcohol includes:
choices: At least 50 hours of community service
questions.explain: Using a fake ID brings at least a $500 fine, 50 hours of service, up to 12 months in jail and a license suspension.
